content: As of August 2023, over 767 million cases of COVID-19 and 6.9 million related deaths have been reported globally. To mitigate the spread of SARS-CoV-2 within schools and prevent further transmission, various public health and social measures were implemented. This study builds upon prior research to evaluate the effectiveness of these measures in maintaining safe school operations during the pandemic. The study aimed to provide an updated analysis of the effectiveness of interventions implemented in school settings to ensure safe, continued operations during the COVID-19 pandemic. Researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, WHO COVID-19 Global Literature database, and others, as of February 18, 2022. Eligible studies focused on interventions targeting students aged 4 to 18 years, school staff, or both, and assessed outcomes related to transmission, as well as intended or unintended consequences. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. For the primary studies, detailed data extraction and bias assessment were performed, while supporting studies underwent minimal data extraction. Findings were synthesized narratively, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated. The review included 15 primary studies, which examined interventions aimed at reducing contacts (4 studies), making contacts safer (7 studies), implementing surveillance and response measures (6 studies), and using multicomponent strategies (1 study). These studies assessed outcomes in school populations, the general population, and adults living with school-attending children. The settings ranged from kindergarten to grade 12 (K-12), secondary schools, and K-8 schools. Most studies were conducted in the WHO Region of the Americas, with a few in the WHO European Region. Measures to Reduce Contact Four studies evaluated interventions to reduce contact, grouped into 21 bodies of evidence with moderate-, low-, or very low-certainty ratings. Remote teaching, compared to in-person or hybrid teaching, showed mixed results. Moderate-certainty evidence suggested no effect on deaths but a reduction in hospitalizations in the general population. However, remote teaching was associated with mostly harmful effects for students and staff. Hybrid teaching showed mixed effects. Very low-certainty evidence indicated that closing playgrounds and cafeterias might have increased infection risk among adults living with schoolchildren, while cancelling extracurricular activities and restricting parental entry had beneficial effects. Measures to Make Contact Safer Seven studies assessed interventions to make contact safer, grouped into eight bodies of evidence. Mask mandates showed low-certainty evidence of a beneficial effect on transmission, with full mandates likely being more effective than partial or no mandates (moderate-certainty evidence). Physical distancing had mixed effects on infection risk among staff and students. Ventilation measures likely reduced cases among staff and students (moderate-certainty evidence). One study suggested that not sharing supplies and increasing desk space might reduce infection risk for adults living with schoolchildren, but desk shields might have harmful effects (very low-certainty evidence). Surveillance and Response Measures Six studies examined surveillance and response measures, grouped into seven bodies of evidence. Daily testing strategies to replace or reduce quarantine likely reduced missed school days and decreased the proportion of asymptomatic school contacts testing positive (moderate-certainty evidence). The performance of rapid antigen detection testing varied widely, with detection rates ranging from 28.6% to 95.8% and positive predictive values from 24.0% to 100.0% (very low-certainty evidence). Moderate-certainty evidence suggested no onward transmission from contacts of positive cases, and replacing or shortening quarantine with testing likely reduced missed school days (low-certainty evidence). Multicomponent Measures One study evaluated multicomponent measures, which may have reduced infection risk among adults living with schoolchildren (very low-certainty evidence). Conclusions The findings suggest that a range of measures can positively impact transmission-related outcomes, healthcare utilization, and school attendance. The certainty of evidence in this review was higher than in the original review. However, further high-quality research across diverse contexts is necessary to develop a more robust, evidence-based understanding of how to safely keep schools open during COVID-19 or similar public health emergencies.
